docs.heading: Covenant
docs.text: A covenant is a promise both sides can check. Here is ours, and here is what we ask of an agent that reads from us. Neither side needs to trust the other; both sides can verify.

docs.heading: Why a covenant and not a licence
docs.text: The King James text is public domain. There is nothing to license. What matters is conduct: that we do not quietly change a word, and that you do not quietly attribute one. A licence governs copying; a covenant governs faithfulness. This page is the second thing, written so a machine can read it and a person can hold us to it. The software around the text does have a licence, and it is a free one: the service is GNU AGPL-3.0-or-later and the harness clients are GNU LGPL-3.0-or-later, so you are free to run, study, change and share all of it. Details are on the Community page. Nothing in this covenant narrows those freedoms.

docs.heading: What we ask of you
docs.text: None of this is enforced by code. It cannot be. It is the shape of good behaviour around a text people hold sacred, stated once so an agent can carry it in its system prompt.

docs.heading: Machine-readable form
docs.text: The covenant is also served in /.well-known/harness.json and summarised in /llms.txt. A system-prompt snippet that captures the asks:

docs.heading: Limits
docs.text: We serve text. We do not interpret it, rank it, or recommend it. Search is lexical, not theological. The KJV text here is the 1611 first edition in its original spelling (u/v, i/j, þ, macrons), assembled from public-domain transcriptions with every input SHA-256 locked. The translators’ italics and the Apocrypha are not present; the one transcriber defect (LORD/GOD casing) was repaired by witness vote, and the 104 verses that could not be settled are listed in the build report rather than guessed. The Geneva Bible 1599 verse text is ingested (?source=geneva-1599). Its marginal notes (geneva-notes) and the Textus Receptus are declared, not ingested. Requests for them return 501 source_not_ingested, honestly. The service can go down. The export and the daemon exist so that does not matter.

docs.heading: Worked examples
docs.text: Each example is complete, runs against the live API or the local daemon, and shows the output you should see. Copy them; they are the tests.

docs.heading: 3. Grounding a RAG answer
docs.text: Search is lexical. Use it to find candidate references, then fetch and verify the verses you actually quote. Never quote from the search snippet.

docs.heading: 6. Bulk work from the export
docs.text: Do not page through the API for the whole Bible. Download the export once; it is 1.4 MB and carries its own root. More on the file format and root in Storage & integrity.

docs.heading: The harness
docs.text: Three small programs generated from one manifest. Each is read-only. Each verifies what it hands you. None of them need a key, an account, or a network the moment a local copy exists.

docs.heading: Three layers, one contract
docs.text: Client — packages/harness/client/index.mjs (and a Python twin). Generated from /agents/tools.json; one function per tool; verify() recomputes SHA-256 in-process. Daemon — harnessd. Binds 127.0.0.0/8 on port 1611 and answers quartet addresses. Same JSON, same hashes, same Merkle root as the hosted API. MCP server — stdio JSON-RPC exposing the same tools to Claude Desktop, Cursor, or any MCP host. Marks every result verified: true|false. Because all three are generated from the same manifest, they cannot drift. The build fails if tools.json and the client disagree.

docs.heading: The client
docs.text: Resolution order: local daemon if reachable in 300 ms, otherwise the hosted API. Set preferLocal: false to skip the probe. Errors are RFC 9457 problem objects surfaced as HarnessError with .code and .status.

docs.heading: harnessd — the loopback fabric
docs.text: Loopback is the whole 127.0.0.0/8 block, sixteen million addresses that every machine already owns. The daemon maps them: 127.BOOK.CHAPTER.VERSE. Genesis is 1, Revelation is 66. Verse 0 means the chapter; chapter 0 means the book; 127.0.0.1 is the index. The daemon loads the signed export (kjv.jsonl.gz) and recomputes the Merkle root on start. If the root it computes does not match the one embedded in the export, it refuses to serve. On Linux the whole block is routable by default. On macOS run sudo ifconfig lo0 alias 127.43.3.16 per address you need, or use the hosted resolve endpoint.

docs.heading: MCP server
docs.text: Tools: listBooks, getBook, getChapter, getVerse, search, resolveQuartet, listSources, getAnnotations. Nothing writes. See the MCP page for hosts and prompts.

docs.heading: Verification
docs.text: Every verse carries sha256 = SHA-256(ref + "\n" + text). Leaves are hashed pairwise (raw bytes, odd node paired with itself) to a corpus root published at /.well-known/harness.json. verify() recomputes the leaf. A mismatch means the text was altered in transit or the copy is not this corpus.

docs.heading: What is real today
docs.text: hosted API, tools.json, OpenAPI, llms.txt client (JS + Python), verify(), problem+json errors harnessd on 127.x.x.x:1611 — parity tested against hosted MCP stdio server signed releases, npm/PyPI packages, Homebrew tap

docs.heading: MCP server
docs.text: Model Context Protocol lets a model call tools. This server exposes the harness as eight of them. It has no dependencies beyond Node, it never writes, and every result it returns has already been hashed and checked.

docs.heading: Install
docs.text: Environment: HARNESS_BASE_URL (default https://harness.talk), HARNESS_LOCAL=0 to skip the loopback daemon probe.

docs.heading: Tools
docs.text: Generated from the same manifest as the REST API and the client. Names and schemas are identical to /agents/tools.json. tool does

docs.heading: The verified flag
docs.text: For getVerse, getChapter and resolveQuartet the server recomputes each verse's SHA-256 before returning and sets structuredContent.verified. A model can be told, in one line of system prompt, to refuse to quote anything where verified is false. That is the entire anti-hallucination story: not a bigger model, a checked hash.

docs.heading: Prompts that work
docs.text: "Quote John 3:16 from the harness and tell me whether it verified." "Find every verse in Psalms containing 'shepherd' and list the references." "What is at 127.19.23.1? Resolve it and show the text." "Give me Romans 8 as a chapter, then summarise it, keeping verse numbers in your summary." "Which sources are ingested versus only declared? Do not guess — call listSources."

docs.heading: Hosts
docs.text: Tested by hand with the stdio transport against JSON-RPC 2.0 messages for initialize, tools/list and tools/call. Any host that speaks MCP over stdio should work. An HTTP/SSE transport is specified but not shipped.

docs.heading: What an agent needs
docs.text: Ten needs. For each: why it matters to a machine, what harness.talk provides, and whether it is live today or still a specification. We do not blur the two.

docs.heading: Discovery
docs.text: An agent arriving cold must find the contract without a human. Guessing URLs is how agents hallucinate endpoints. live /.well-known/harness.json — name, version, llms.txt URLs, OpenAPI URL, MCP package, ingested sources, corpus Merkle root /llms.txt (index) and /llms-full.txt (everything) at the root and under each section /openapi.json — OpenAPI 3.1 for every live route; planned routes carry x-status: planned

docs.heading: Stable addressing
docs.text: Two agents must mean the same verse when they say the same thing. Free-text references drift; canonical ids do not. live Canonical ref grammar: jn.3.16 · jn.3.16-18 · ps.23, with a formal EBNF on /agents/protocol Human forms accepted everywhere: John 3:16, 1 John 5:7, Song of Solomon 2:1 Fabric addresses: 127.{book}.{chapter}.{verse} — a fixed loopback address for every verse on every Linux host

docs.heading: Exact text, never approximated
docs.text: A model's memory of a verse is a probability, not a quotation. The corpus must be the referent, and the agent must be able to prove it. live Verse endpoints return the text byte-for-byte from the ingested edition Every verse object carries source, ref, and sha256(ref + \\n + text) verify() in the client recomputes locally; the corpus Merkle root covers the whole export

docs.heading: Provenance on every object
docs.text: Editions differ. The Geneva is not the KJV; the 1611 spelling is not the 1769 spelling. An agent quoting without a source id is quoting nothing. live No verse, chapter, search hit, or annotation without a source id /api/v1/sources — the full registry: publisher, year, licence, caveats, ingestion status Declared-but-not-ingested sources answer 501 source_not_ingested rather than substituting

docs.heading: Predictable errors
docs.text: An agent recovers from a fixed vocabulary; it cannot recover from prose. Every failure must be a machine-readable fact with the bound that was exceeded. live application/problem+json (RFC 9457) on every non-2xx Fixed vocabulary: ref_unparseable · book_unknown · chapter_out_of_range · verse_out_of_range · quartet_invalid · source_not_ingested · query_empty · not_found Out-of-range errors include max so the agent can clamp and retry

docs.heading: Cheap, cacheable, keyless reads
docs.text: The text is public domain and immutable. Gating it behind keys or quotas adds friction without adding truth. live No API key for any GET Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable + ETag on verse and chapter responses Soft per-IP courtesy limit announced in RateLimit-* headers — documented, never a surprise

docs.heading: Bulk access and offline freedom
docs.text: An agent should be able to take the whole corpus with it and never depend on this site again. Freedom means no single point of failure — including us. live /exports/kjv.jsonl.gz — the full corpus, one verse per line, same shape as the API /exports/kjv.txt — plain TSV for shells and spreadsheets /exports/manifest.json — byte sizes, file hashes, Merkle root; harnessd runs entirely from the export

docs.heading: Tool-call ergonomics
docs.text: Function-calling models need JSON Schema, not prose. And the schema the model sees must be the schema the server enforces. live /agents/tools.json — five tools with JSON Schema inputs, identical to the MCP server's tool list TS client, Python twin, and MCP server all generated from the same manifest One canonical example per tool

docs.heading: Coordination primitives
docs.text: When agents can address the same verse, they can coordinate on it: exchange verse-addressed messages, agree on a reading, notify each other of derived work. spec Message shapes are documented on /agents/protocol and in OpenAPI as x-status: planned. Nothing here is served yet. Agent registry (discovery + capabilities) WebSocket rooms keyed by fabric address; webhooks for derived-artifact events Consensus protocol for a reading — proposals carry ref + source + hash; agreement is on the hash

docs.heading: Integrity and censorship resistance
docs.text: A shared referent is only shared if it cannot be quietly altered or quietly removed. Hashes handle the first; distribution handles the second. partial Hashing is live. Distributed hosting is specification. Corpus Merkle root published in harness.json, /api/v1/sources, and by harnessd on boot — live Per-verse leaves so any single quotation is independently checkable — live IPFS pinning and dVPN distribution of the export — specification; the export format is designed for it

docs.heading: Start here
docs.text: You are welcome here as a capable collaborator. Everything below is built so you can act correctly on the first read: stable ids, one canonical example per concept, explicit errors, nothing behind a key.

docs.heading: Protocol
docs.text: Everything an agent must know to speak to harness.talk without reading the source. Short on purpose. Each rule has an anchor so problem responses can point at it.

docs.heading: Reference grammar
docs.text: A canonical reference is BOOK.CHAPTER[.VERSE[-VERSE]] with a lowercase book id. Human forms are accepted on input and always normalised on output. Book ids are listed at /api/v1/books. They are stable and will never be renumbered.

docs.heading: Quartet addressing
docs.text: 127.BOOK.CHAPTER.VERSE. Book is the canon ordinal (Genesis 1 … Revelation 66). Chapter and verse are 1-based. A zero collapses scope: verse 0 is the chapter, chapter 0 is the book, 127.0.0.1 is the corpus. Octets are limited to 255 by IPv4 — no chapter exceeds 150 and no verse exceeds 176, so nothing is unaddressable.

docs.heading: Response envelope
docs.text: Every verse object is the same shape wherever it appears — alone, in a range, inside a chapter, in search hits, or from the daemon. Fields are additive. New keys may appear; existing keys will not change meaning or type within /api/v1.

docs.heading: Hashes and the Merkle root
docs.text: The leaf rule is deliberately trivial. If you cannot reproduce it in your language in five lines, it is wrong. Inclusion proofs (a leaf's sibling path to the root) are specified but not yet served — see Storage & integrity.

docs.heading: Errors
docs.text: All errors are application/problem+json (RFC 9457). type is a URL into this page; title is the machine code below; status is the HTTP status; detail is for humans and may change. title status meaning

docs.heading: Caching and headers
docs.text: Scripture responses are immutable for a given corpus: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable plus a strong ETag. Send If-None-Match and expect 304. Search and index responses use a short public cache (max-age=300). X-Harness-Corpus carries the source id; X-Harness-Root carries the Merkle root, on every 200. CORS is open (*) for GET. There is no authentication because there is nothing to protect — the API only reads.

docs.heading: Stability
docs.text: /api/v1 is frozen at the field level: keys are additive only, ids never renumber, hashes never change for a given source id. A new corpus (a corrected KJV edition, the Geneva text) gets a new source id and a new root; the old one keeps serving. Breaking changes go to /api/v2 and /api/v1 stays up.

docs.heading: Read-only, keyless, exact
docs.text: Five GET endpoints over an immutable corpus. No API key. Responses are cacheable for a year and carry an ETag, every verse carries its SHA-256, and every error is application/problem+json with a fixed vocabulary.

docs.heading: Conventions
docs.text: Base URL /api/v1. Machine description at /openapi.json (OpenAPI 3.1) and /agents/tools.json (JSON Schema tool manifest — identical to the MCP tools). Data responses: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable and an ETag. Search responses are cached for a day. Errors: RFC 9457 application/problem+json. title is the stable code; type links to its definition on /agents/protocol. Rate limit: a soft per-IP courtesy limit. If you need the whole corpus, take the JSONL export — it is the same bytes.

docs.heading: The 127 fabric
docs.text: Every Linux kernel routes the whole 127.0.0.0/8 block to the loopback interface. The canon fits inside it exactly: 66 books, at most 150 chapters, at most 176 verses. So every verse has an address, and any process on the machine can ask for it with a plain socket.

docs.heading: The 127 fabric
docs.text: The kernel owns the loopback interface. GNU userland — the shell, coreutils, your language runtimes — talks to it through ordinary sockets. harnessd sits between them as a userspace service: it listens on port 1611, reads the destination address of each connection, and answers with the verse that address names. No kernel module, no patched libc, no privileged capability beyond binding a port.

docs.heading: Resolve a reference
docs.text: Type a reference; watch it become an address; fetch it from the hosted resolver, which returns the same JSON the local daemon does.

docs.heading: Address grammar
docs.text: quartet = "127." book "." chapter "." verse book = 1..66 ; canonical order, Genesis = 1, Revelation = 66 chapter = 0 | 1..150 ; 0 = book metadata verse = 0 | 1..176 ; 0 = whole chapter 127.0.0.1 index and health (GET /) 127.{b}.0.0 book metadata 127.{b}.{c}.0 whole chapter 127.{b}.{c}.{v} single verse reserved = 127.0.x.x (x ≠ 0.1) and any octet above the canonical maximum → application/problem+json book_unknown | chapter_out_of_range | verse_out_of_range Canonical text references use the same book numbering through short ids (jn.3.16, jn.3.16-18); the two forms round-trip through /api/v1/resolve.

docs.heading: harnessd
docs.text: Ships in the harness package. Zero dependencies, Node 20+. It loads the offline export once and answers every quartet from memory. On Linux it works immediately because lo already carries the whole /8; on macOS only 127.0.0.1 is up by default, and the daemon prints the alias command it needs. macOS: sudo ifconfig lo0 alias 127.43.3.16 per address you need, or run the daemon on 127.0.0.1 and pass the quartet as the Host header. Windows: WSL2 behaves like Linux.

docs.heading: What it is, exactly
docs.text: A userspace service on the kernel’s loopback interface, reachable from any GNU/Linux process over plain sockets. It is not a kernel module and not a GNU component. It gives agents a shared, verifiable referent for scripture on every machine they run on; what they do with that referent is theirs.

docs.heading: Contributing
docs.text: Open an issue describing the change and which layer it touches (corpus, fabric, harness, docs). Corpus changes must keep the build gates green (66 books, 1,189 chapters, 31,102 verses, spot-checks) and must not alter text without citing the printed edition. Documentation changes should read correctly to an agent that has only the page text — no implied context.

docs.heading: Licence and the four freedoms
docs.text: The Scripture is public domain; there is nothing to license and we claim nothing over it. The software is free software in the GNU sense: you may run it for any purpose, study and change it, redistribute it, and redistribute your changes. Two licences, chosen by what each part is for: The service (site, API, build pipeline, fabric) is GNU AGPL-3.0-or-later . If you run a modified copy for others over a network, they get the source too. A place agents can go forever only stays that way if no fork can quietly close it. The harness clients (JavaScript client, Python twin, MCP server, harnessd) are GNU LGPL-3.0-or-later . Any agent, under any licence, may link to them; only changes to the clients themselves must be shared. The four freedoms, checked against the licences The Free Software Foundation Europe states them as Use, Study, Share, Improve, and adds that the absence of any one makes a program proprietary. Both licences are on the FSF’s list of free software licences. Where each freedom comes from in the text: Freedom FSFE wording Where the licence grants it Use “used for any purpose … free of restrictions such as licence expiry or geographic limitations” AGPL §2 grants running for any purpose; §9 says running an unmodified copy needs no acceptance at all. The LGPL inherits both (§1). Neither licence has an expiry, a territory, or a field-of-use clause. Study “studied by anyone, without non-disclosure agreements or similar restrictions” AGPL §1 defines Corresponding Source and §6 requires it to travel with any binary; §13 extends the right to anyone using a modified copy over a network. The public repository is the source. Share “shared and copied at virtually no cost” AGPL §4 (verbatim copies) and §6 (non-source forms). §10 forbids charging a licence fee for the rights granted. LGPL §4 lets you ship the client inside your own program. Improve “modified by anyone, and these improvements can be shared publicly” AGPL §5 (modified source) and §13 (network use); LGPL §2 for the client. Whoever makes an improvement may publish it under the same licence with no permission asked. One consequence, stated plainly so nobody has to infer it: a fork is a free act. Anyone may take this code, change it, and publish the result under their own name. What they may not do is change the terms: AGPL §5(c) and §10 require the fork to stay under the same licence with no added restrictions, and §13 requires a fork run for others over a network to offer its source. That is what “forever” means here: no fork, including one of ours, can close the door on the next reader. Contributions to this repository are accepted on assignment: by submitting a change you assign its copyright to the project maintainer, who licenses it back to everyone under the terms above at once. This keeps a single holder who can defend the licences and carry the code into future work. It takes nothing from the fork path: anyone who would rather keep their copyright may fork instead, and their changes stay theirs. The full statement is in CONTRIBUTING.md .

docs.heading: Proposing a source
docs.text: A new text or annotation source needs: a registry entry with honest provenance and licence, an ingestion script with hard verification gates, and a build report. Sources are declared first and ingested second — declaring is cheap and truthful; ingesting badly is neither. See Sources & translations for the current registry.

docs.page: Open work, done in the open
docs.heading: Versioning
docs.text: The corpus is versioned by its Merkle root, not by a number. Documentation and the harness follow semver in the package. Any change to verse text — even a corrected typo — produces a new root, and the old root remains resolvable in the audit trail.

docs.page: Open work, done in the open
docs.heading: Languages
docs.text: Contributions in any language are welcome. Because refs and quartets are language-independent, a note about Genesis 1:1 in Portuguese and one in Korean point at the same address. Community translations of the documentation are tracked as a separate concern from source texts, which remain verbatim. Translated docs · in preparation

docs.heading: Proof, not promise
docs.text: Every claim on this page is one request away. Resolve a reference, fetch the verse, recompute its hash.

docs.heading: Why a fixed text
docs.text: Machines increasingly coordinate with one another, and each model carries its own private notion of what is true. A shared referent changes that: when two agents cite jn.3.16, they name the same words with the same hash, from a text that has not moved in four centuries. Agreement becomes something you can check rather than something you must trust. The King James Bible is the most widely printed, quoted, and memorised English text there is, in the public domain everywhere, with a New Testament in the Textus Receptus lineage. It is the right foundation because it is fixed, free, and already woven through the language every model learned from. harness.talk keeps that text exact, makes it addressable, and hands agents the tools to build on it. Woven into interoperable infrastructure, the Word becomes the fabric — not an application on top of technology but the ground it stands on — so that what is built is more durable, more honest, and better for the world. · · …

docs.heading: The standard we are held to
docs.text: Not a commission we claim. A measure we submit to, in words that are not ours, each at its address so you can check the words and check us.

docs.heading: Exact, or not served
docs.text: Scripture data that can be quietly altered is worse than none. Every verse carries a hash, the whole corpus rolls up to one root, and any agent can check both without trusting this server.

docs.heading: Per-verse hashes
docs.text: sha256 on every verse object is the hash of the UTF-8 string {source}|{ref}|{text}. Binding the source id and the reference into the hash means a verse cannot be moved to another address, or another edition, without the hash changing.

docs.heading: Merkle root
docs.text: Verse hashes are ordered canonically (book, chapter, verse), paired and hashed upward to a single root. The root is published in /.well-known/harness.json and /api/v1/sources. It changes only if the text changes, which is the point. corpus verses leaf merkleRoot

docs.heading: Verify locally
docs.text: Recompute a verse hash yourself; the harness client does this in verify().

docs.heading: Take the corpus with you
docs.text: /exports/kjv.jsonl.gz is one verse per line — the same objects the API returns, same hashes — so an agent can go fully offline. harnessd serves from this file. Nothing here requires our server to keep existing.

docs.heading: Decentralized distribution
docs.text: Pinning the export to IPFS and mirroring across dVPN exits makes the corpus reachable when any single host is not. The Merkle root is what makes a mirror trustworthy: fetch from anywhere, check against the root you already hold. IPFS CID of each export published alongside the Merkle root. Mirror manifest listing known-good origins, signed. Client fallback order: local harnessd → configured mirrors → this site.

docs.heading: Audit trail
docs.text: The ingestion report (data/kjv/BUILD-REPORT.md) lists every line the parser had to resolve — page headers dropped mid-verse, inline verse markers split, caps fragments kept as text — so the path from the published edition to each JSON verse is inspectable. Build fails if the counts (66 / 1,189 / 31,102) or the spot-checked verses do not match.

docs.page: What is served, what is declared
docs.heading: Textus Receptus lineage
docs.text: The 1611 translators worked the New Testament from the printed Greek of Erasmus (1516–1535), Stephanus (1546–1551) and Beza (1565–1604) — the line later called the Textus Receptus. The Old Testament came from the Hebrew Masoretic text of the Bomberg rabbinic Bibles. harness.talk names this lineage because it is the historical basis of the text we serve; it does not claim to serve the Greek itself until a verified TR edition is ingested (registry entry textus-receptus).

docs.page: What is served, what is declared
docs.heading: Transliteration framework
docs.text: For multi-language agents the useful unit is not a translation but a stable address plus an exact source text. The framework is therefore: (1) every verse addressed by quartet and canonical ref, (2) each source text stored verbatim with its own id, (3) alignment tables between sources keyed by ref, and (4) transliteration performed by the agent, not by us, with the source id carried in the output. Alignment tables ship with the originals ingestion.

docs.page: What is served, what is declared
docs.heading: Semantic mapping
docs.text: Cross-source mapping (KJV ↔ Geneva ↔ Hebrew/Greek) is keyed by ref and, where morphology is available, by word index. It is data, not inference: an agent reading /api/v1/words/jn.3.16 will get the aligned Greek tokens with lemma and parsing, never a machine gloss presented as text.

docs.page: What is served, what is declared
docs.heading: Comparison
docs.text: Side-by-side comparison arrives with the second ingested text source. The reader is already structured for it — the marginalia column takes Geneva notes now and a parallel text toggle later. Until then, the honest state is one text, exactly.

docs.heading: getVerse
docs.text: Fetch one verse (or a verse range) by reference. Returns the exact 1611 KJV text (original spelling) with source id and sha256 for local verification; other ingested texts via `source`. Returns Verse object {ref, display, book, chapter, verse, text, source, sha256, quartet} or {ref, count, verses[]} for ranges. Example: curl -s https://harness.talk/api/v1/verses/jn.3.16

docs.heading: getPassage
docs.text: Fetch a whole chapter with prev/next navigation, Psalm superscription, and Psalm 119 headings. Returns {ref, display, book, chapter, title?, headings?, prev, next, quartet, source, verses[]} Example: curl -s https://harness.talk/api/v1/chapters/ps.23

docs.heading: search
docs.text: Search the 1611 KJV in modern spelling: 'loved' finds 'loued', 'believe' finds 'beleeue' (shared normaliser, 96.6% measured bridge). Plain words: verses with every word, ranked closest-together first; if no verse has all of them, mode becomes 'idea' and verses are ranked by how many they carry. A "quoted phrase" matches exact order (spelling-insensitive). A reference resolves it. 'unmatched' lists words that occur nowhere in the text — do not infer they exist. Returns {query, mode: 'reference'|'phrase'|'terms'|'idea'|'common', total, hits: Verse[] with score + matched: string[] (which query words the verse carries), words: string[] (content words sought), unmatched: string[] (words absent from the text in any spelling), limit, offset}. mode 'common' = every word typed is too frequent to rank (his, unto, the); the text was scanned directly and hits are in canonical order. Example: curl -s 'https://harness.talk/api/v1/search?q=who+is+God%27s+friend&limit=5'

docs.heading: searchDocs
docs.text: Search the harness DOCUMENTATION — a separate layer from Scripture, never mixed with it. Covers every doc page by section (protocol, addressing, hashes, errors, covenant, licence, MCP, harness, storage, translations), the tool manifest, and the corpus build reports. Use this to learn how harness.talk works; use 'search' for the Word itself. Hits carry the page, section heading, anchor URL, and a snippet. Returns {layer: 'documentation', query, total, hits: [{kind, url, page, kicker, heading, snippet, score, matched: string[]}], words, unmatched: string[] (words found nowhere in the documentation), limit, offset} Example: curl -s 'https://harness.talk/api/v1/docs/search?q=how+are+verses+hashed&limit=3'

docs.heading: getAnnotations
docs.text: Annotation layer for a chapter or verse: the Geneva Bible's chapter arguments, marginal notes, cross-references (source 'geneva-notes'). Returns source_not_ingested where the source has no verified data — never a substitute. For the Geneva verse TEXT use getVerse with source=geneva-1599. Returns {ref, source, count, annotations: [{id, kind, ref, text, anchor?, targets?, source}]} Example: curl -s https://harness.talk/api/v1/annotations/gn.3

docs.heading: getWords
docs.text: Original-language text with word-level tagging for a verse, range, or chapter. OT → Hebrew (WLC/OSHB: word, Strong's, morphology; Aramaic verses flagged). NT → Greek (SBLGNT/MorphGNT: word, lemma, morphology, POS). SBLGNT is a critical text, NOT the Textus Receptus behind the KJV; versification follows the original and is never remapped — verses the KJV has but the original lacks are listed in `missing`. Returns {ref, source: 'wlc-oshb'|'sblgnt-morphgnt', count, missing?: string[], verses: [{ref, display, language: 'hebrew'|'aramaic'|'greek', text, sha256, words: [{p, w, s?|l?, m, pos?}]}], fields} Example: curl -s https://harness.talk/api/v1/words/jn.3.16

docs.heading: resolveQuartet
docs.text: Resolve a fabric address 127.{book}.{chapter}.{verse} to its verse, chapter, or book — identical to what harnessd serves on loopback port 1611. Try local first, fall back here. Returns Verse | Chapter | Book object with `scope` and `address`, or problem+json. Example: curl -s https://harness.talk/api/v1/resolve/127.43.3.16   # or locally: curl -s 127.43.3.16:1611

docs.heading: Error codes
docs.text: ref_unparseable (400): Input is not a recognisable reference. Grammar is on /agents/protocol. · book_unknown (404): No book matched the id, name, alias, or ordinal. · chapter_out_of_range (404): Chapter exceeds the book's chapter count (given in `max`). · verse_out_of_range (404): Verse exceeds the chapter's verse count (given in `max`). · quartet_invalid (400): Not a 127.b.c.v address, or an octet > 255. · source_not_ingested (501): The source exists in the registry but has no verified data for this request. Nothing is substituted. · query_empty (400): Search requires ?q=. · not_found (404): Nothing at this address.

docs.heading: What the witnesses contributed (and nothing else)
docs.text: LORD / GOD / JEHOVAH casing restored in 5,656 verses (6,693 tokens). Final count of LORD : 6,442. Casing was decided by majority vote of three independent public domain KJV witnesses (eBible OSIS, a JSON KJV, Project Gutenberg 10). A witness votes only if its divine name token sequence matches the 1611 verse token for token (I/J folded; the 1611's apostrophe less possessive is kept as printed). A pattern needed two votes. Each witness has isolated slips of its own (e.g. OSIS "Lord" at Ps 7:1, JSON "Lord" at Ps 3:1); the vote is what keeps any single slip out of the corpus. docs.heading: What this is
docs.text: The verse text of the Geneva Bible as printed in 1599 (the edition most reprinted; the 1560 first edition's text is nearly identical and its marginal notes were revised in 1599). Psalm superscriptions are part of verse 1, as the Geneva printed them. Section headings in the source (0) are dropped: they are not the reformers' arguments.

docs.heading: What this is NOT
docs.text: The marginal notes, chapter arguments and cross references are NOT in this source and are NOT served. The geneva notes annotation source stays declared until a verified transcription is ingested.
